experiment.title: MongoDB on its home ground: where does it fit Odin?
experiment.summary: Our two MongoDB studies (EXP 013 and EXP 014) tested PostgreSQL's home ground: one node, bounded JSON, partial updates and dynamic-attribute queries. This study tests MongoDB's. It takes the four pain points Odin has on record (EXP 010's design study, section 1): key order in hash-chained records, a change feed that survives restarts, expiry on append-only data, and aggregation over document values. Each store gets its best realistic design, checked by one reviewer arguing for each store. The verdict is per scenario; there is no overall winner.
experiment.note: Written, hashed and merged to main before any counted run. Counted runs start only after the commit that publishes this record. Nothing in this record may change afterwards; a later change is a new, dated amendment, published first.

relation.why: EXP 013 and EXP 014 asked whether MongoDB is faster at what PostgreSQL already does well, with PostgreSQL given its strongest tested design each time. They did not test what MongoDB is built for. Each of Odin's four recorded pain points maps onto a native MongoDB mechanism, and none was measured. EXP 013 and EXP 014 stand as published; this experiment does not change or replace them.

question: On Odin's four recorded pain points (odin-rnd EXP 010 design study, section 1), which store solves each one correctly, with fewer operational components, at equal or better cost, when each gets its best realistic design? The verdict is per scenario. There is no overall winner.

arms.setup: A one-member replica set (replSet, rs.initiate); auth on with a keyFile; writes w: majority, j: true.
The official image, plus pinned derived images where an extension is used (wal2json, pg_cron, pg_partman); synchronous_commit = on. Each scenario also runs a no-extension variant.
arms.tuning: shared_buffers 1 GB, effective_cache_size 2 GB, work_mem 64 MB, max_parallel_workers_per_gather 2, --shm-size 1 GB

pinning: Arms are pinned before the first counted run; image tags and digests are recorded in the run manifest.

equalResources.limits: The same --memory / --cpus on both arms: 4 GB / 2 CPU per database container.
equalResources.tuning: Explicit on both arms, as listed per arm.
equalResources.compression: The defaults on both (snappy, pglz), recorded.

host.storage: Data is on named volumes on the WSL2 ext4 disk, never on NTFS bind mounts.
host.fsync: pg_test_fsync and fio --fsync=1 are run inside each container and recorded, together with mongod's filesystem warning.
host.client: The client runs in a container on the same Docker network, with equal pool sizes.
host.replication: A macOS machine runs the same frozen source as a second-OS replication.

data.kind: Synthetic, sized from Odin's recorded memory store (~15.5k rows / 270 MB).
data.beforeEachCell: PostgreSQL runs VACUUM ANALYZE and CHECKPOINT. The cache state is the same for both arms (warm, after one discarded pass). Checkpoint and autovacuum events are logged.

scenarios.name: Order-preserving records
scenarios.data: Hash-chained events; the payload is a nested field in authored key order.

arms.mongodb: BSON, decoded to dict; RawBSONDocument is used for a byte check.
arms.postgresql: A json column with expression GIN / B-tree indexes on (payload::jsonb …); variant: a stored generated jsonb column.
arms.both: One serializer rule for both arms (keys in stored order).

scenarios.gate: 100% of chains verify over the bytes the client reads back, and the nested queries (dot-notation / expression paths only) equal the oracle.

scenarios.name: A durable, resumable change feed

arms.mongodb: watch() with a $match; the post-batch resume token persisted; startAfter; the driver's automatic resume.
arms.postgresql-a: Logical decoding with pgoutput, resuming from confirmed_flush_lsn.
arms.both: Either side may persist the token / cursor with the effect in one transaction.

scenarios.faults: The consumer is killed at seeded points; the database restarts once per cell; the consumer is down for a frozen 10 minutes.
scenarios.retention: Oplog and slot are given the same disk budget (oplogMinRetentionHours / size against max_slot_wal_keep_size). Lost history is classified the same in both arms.
scenarios.primary: End-to-end lag p95, with maxAwaitTimeMS, batch size and the poll interval frozen and recorded.

scenarios.name: TTL on append-only data
scenarios.appendOnly: The application role cannot update or delete. It holds INSERT, SELECT only (PostgreSQL) or a custom role with find + insert (MongoDB). An application update must fail (permission denied / code 13).

arms.mongodb: A TTL index, expireAfterSeconds: 0, on expireAt.
arms.postgresql: Range partitions on expires_at with DETACH CONCURRENTLY + DROP, or an owner-role batched DELETE (index on expires_at).
arms.scheduling: By pg_cron or a sidecar; the no-extension variant always runs.
arms.both: A read filter (expireAt > now / row-level security) is allowed on both arms.

cells.cadence: Tuned cadences, 5 s (ttlMonitorSleepSecs = 5, a 5 s sweep).

scenarios.gate: No expired record visible past the grace; the append-only rule is never bypassed by the application role.
scenarios.reported: Physical and visible expiry lag p50 / p95, and write p95 during expiry.

scenarios.name: Server-side aggregation over document values

arms.mongodb: A pipeline with $match / $sort first, $group, $facet or separate concurrent pipelines, allowDiskUse explicit.
arms.postgresql: SQL over JSONB with GROUP BY / GROUPING SETS / FILTER, LATERAL jsonb_to_recordset, and expression or generated columns.
arms.baseline: Odin's current pattern (fetch and aggregate in the application).
arms.both: Matching index allowances on both arms.

scenarios.reported: Application peak memory, bytes over the wire, and 1×.

repetitions: 5 paired repetitions per cell, with the arm order alternating, plus a separate-seed reproduction of every cell.

components.rule: A frozen checklist; both counts published. One component each for:
checklist: every process or container beyond the database server;
every server setting changed off its default and needed for correctness;
every persistent non-data object: a slot, publication, trigger, policy, partition scheme (one per scheme), TTL index, custom role or keyFile;
every safety alarm an operator must watch (an oplog window, slot retention).
components.eachPays: MongoDB pays for its replica set, keyFile, oplog sizing and oplog alarm. PostgreSQL pays for its slot, publication, wal_level, jobs and partitions.

verdicts.mongodb-fits / postgres-fits: The store passes the gate, and either: beats the other store's best variant on the primary latency metric by ≥ 20 % on the median, in ≥ 4 of 5 paired repetitions, with the same direction in the reproduction; or, for S3, and as a tie-break for S2, has at least 2 fewer components.
verdicts.both-fit: Both pass, and neither condition holds.
verdicts.invalid: A cell is incomplete, or source / durability drifted.

decision.publication: Every cell, every variant, every outcome.

predictions.frozen: Frozen with this record, from three parties, so the result can contradict them.

designAuthor.who: The design author (draft predictions, corrected after the reviews).
designAuthor.S1: both-fit (the draft's "json loses indexing" was wrong)

reviews.how: Before the freeze, one independent model reviewer (Claude, fresh context) argued for MongoDB's best realistic design and one for PostgreSQL's, each allowed to veto a strawman. Every veto was accepted; FREEZE-NOTES.md lists each veto and its resolution, and where the two reviewers differed.
